title: Menstrual cycle-dependent changes in neuromuscular control during a functional single-leg landing task in physically active women.
summary:
Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries occur during sports without direct body contact more frequently in physically active women than in male athletes. The interplay of the anterior and posterior thigh muscles, that is, the knee extensors and knee flexors, plays a central role in knee stability during such landing movements. Both muscle groups are activated in a coordinated manner before and during the landing and jointly stabilize the knee. When this interplay fails, for example because the muscles are activated too late or in an uncoordinated manner, the shin bone may slide forward during the landing and thereby heavily load the anterior cruciate ligament. Insufficiently coordinated activation of these muscles is therefore considered one of the mechanisms contributing to anterior cruciate ligament injury. How these muscles are controlled, may be influenced by the natural fluctuations of the female sex hormones across the menstrual cycle. This study therefore examines whether the timing of muscle activation and the interplay of these two muscle groups during a single-leg landing task differ between phases of the menstrual cycle.

A total of 20 physically active women with a regular natural menstrual cycle will participate in the study. The number of participants was determined a priori with a power analysis. During the first cycle, the participants keep a daily cycle calendar and use ovulation tests in the form of urine tests at home. In the subsequent cycle, three measurement sessions take place, each in a different phase of the menstrual cycle. These three phases were chosen because the concentrations of the two sex hormones, estradiol and progesterone, differ from phase to phase. In the first phase, both hormones are present at low concentrations. In the second, mainly estradiol is elevated, while in the third both progesterone and estradiol are elavated. This enables to associate possible differences in muscle activation to the respective hormonal profiles. At these sessions, the electrical activity of the thigh muscles is measured during a standardized single-leg landing from a 30 cm high box. To determine the concentrations of the female sex hormones estradiol and progesterone, a little volume of capillary blood is taken from the fingertip at each session.

This study aims to contribute to a better understanding of how knee staibilizing muscles  are controlled in physically active women across the menstrual cycle. The results may also support future research on injury prevention.
conditions: Healthy, eumenorrheic, physically active women without any diseases; the study examines neuromuscular control (muscle activation) during a single-leg-landing task across the phases of the menstrual cycle.

interventions.name:
Single-arm observational study:

A total of 20 healthy, eumenorrheic and physically active women aged 18 to 35 years will be included. The study comprises two consecutive menstrual cycles per participant.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Eumenorrheic menstrual cycle with regular cycle length of 21-35 days

No use of hormonal contraceptives

Physically active (regular training, at least 2 sessions per week for at least 6 months)

Written informed consent after full study information
Exclusion criteria:
Pregnancy or breastfeeding

Irregular cycle or cycle length below 21 or above 35 days

Known gynaecological, endocrinological, or neurological condition with possible influence on the menstrual cycle or neuromuscular control (e.g. PCOS, endometriosis, thyroid disorders, diabetes mellitus, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy)

Acute injuries or complaints of the lower extremities preventing correct or pain-free performance of the task

Capillary blood hormone concentrations not matching the intended cycle phase (verified a posteriori after the measurements).
